read: full (all 29 pages: main text pp. 1-13, references pp. 13-15, Appendices A-I pp. 16-29)
venue_now: The text file is arXiv 2305.20050v1, 31 May 2023 (p. 1 footer), and shows no venue; the arXiv record in notes/arxiv_abs_check.json has only v1. papers.json records ICLR 2024 (poster), which the text cannot confirm. The May entry cites the arXiv preprint.
what_it_is: An OpenAI method-and-dataset paper comparing outcome supervision (a label on the final answer) with process supervision (a human label on every step) for training reward models that rank solutions sampled from a GPT-4-based generator on MATH (pp. 1-3). Human data-labellers marked each step of model-generated solutions positive, negative or neutral, giving PRM800K: about 800K step labels on 75K solutions to 12K problems (p. 4). Reward models are compared by best-of-N selection graded on the final answer: the process-supervised reward model (PRM) picks a correct solution for 78.2% of a 500-problem MATH test subset at N = 1860, against 72.4% for the outcome-supervised model (ORM) and 69.6% for majority voting (p. 7). Small-scale experiments use the large PRM as a synthetic labeller to isolate the supervision type, and show that active learning is about 2.6 times more data-efficient (pp. 8-9).
domain: competition mathematics (MATH), with an out-of-distribution check on AP Calculus, AP Chemistry, AP Physics and AMC10/12 questions (p. 10)
size: PRM800K: about 800K step labels on 75K solutions to 12K problems after filtering (p. 4); 1,085,590 labels on 101,599 solutions before filtering (p. 17). Test set: the 500 MATH test problems not moved into training (p. 5, p. 18). OOD set: '224 STEM questions' in the text, while Table 1's rows sum to 234 (p. 10). Models: a GPT-4-based large-scale generator and reward models, and small-scale models pretrained with about 200 times less compute (p. 3).
source_of_items: existing MATH problems (Hendrycks et al., 2021); the solutions are sampled from the paper's own generator and labelled by human data-labellers (pp. 3-4)
has_gold_traces: partial: human step-correctness labels (positive, negative, neutral) on model-generated solutions, stopping at the first negative step in phase 2 (p. 6, p. 19). Labellers were given the final answer but no reference solution (p. 19); no gold trace is used to score steps.
evaluation: final answer: reward models are scored by best-of-N search, in which the top-ranked of N sampled solutions is graded automatically on its final answer (p. 3). The PRM itself scores steps (solution score = product of step-correctness probabilities, p. 6, p. 20), but the paper reports no step-level accuracy of the PRM against held-out human labels; step-level behaviour is shown only through selected examples (pp. 23-29).
human_validation: Labellers were screened on 30 quality-control questions and admitted only if they agreed with the researchers' gold labels at least 75% of the time; 10 to 20 further quality-control problems per generation were served to remove labellers whose quality slipped (pp. 17-18). The text reports no inter-annotator agreement coefficient.
contamination_measures: MathMix was decontaminated against the MATH test split by string and n-gram matching, with 'no strong guarantees' (p. 11, p. 16); the PRM's advantage is re-checked on recent AP and AMC exams released after the pre-training data was compiled (p. 10).

engtrace_use.sentence: Inspired by recent advances in process supervision (Lightman et al., 2023) and cascaded model verification (Chen et al., 2023), we introduce a two-stage evaluation framework that validates intermediate reasoning steps in addition to final-answer accuracy through a tiered verification protocol. (Section 4, L390-395)
engtrace_use.explanation: The sentence credits Lightman et al. only with 'advances in process supervision', and the paper is exactly that: it shows that process supervision trains more reliable reward models than outcome supervision on MATH (abstract p. 1; contributions p. 2; conclusion p. 13) and releases PRM800K (p. 4). 'Inspired by' makes no further claim about the paper. Two cautions for the rewrite. (1) In the paper, process supervision is human step-level feedback used to train a reward model, and reward models are judged by best-of-N selection graded on final answers (p. 3, Section 2.1); it is not an evaluation protocol for comparing LLMs, so EngTrace's use of the term for checking steps against gold traces is an extension the text should state rather than imply. (2) The sentence describes a 'two-stage ... tiered verification protocol' that the deterministic evaluator has replaced, so it must be rewritten anyway, and 'recent' is dated for a 2023 paper. The reference entry is wrong: it prints 30 names, while the paper lists 10 authors (p. 1: Lightman, Kosaraju, Burda, Edwards, Baker, Lee, Leike, Schulman, Sutskever, Cobbe); 23 of the printed names are not authors and Baker, Lee and Cobbe are missing (citation map C-S). The key is unaffected.

suggested_wording: Lightman et al. (2023) showed that process supervision, feedback on every intermediate step rather than on the final answer alone, trains more reliable reward models than outcome supervision on MATH, and released PRM800K, 800K step-level labels written by human labellers because step correctness, unlike a final answer, could not be checked automatically.
facts_to_cite: Outcome supervision gives feedback on the final result; process supervision gives feedback on each intermediate reasoning step (p. 1).

Process supervision trains more reliable reward models than outcome supervision on MATH: at best-of-1860 the PRM selects a correct solution for 78.2% of a 500-problem MATH test subset, against 72.4% for the ORM and 69.6% for majority voting (p. 7, Figure 3; subset described p. 18).
PRM800K holds about 800K human step-level labels on 75K model-generated solutions to 12K MATH problems (p. 4); 1,085,590 labels on 101,599 solutions before filtering (p. 17).
Each step is labelled positive, negative or neutral (p. 4); in phase 2, labelling stops at the first negative step (p. 6, p. 19).
Human labellers were needed because MATH final answers are automatically checkable but 'there is no simple way to automate process supervision' (p. 3).
Final-answer grading credits solutions that reach the correct answer with incorrect reasoning (p. 5, p. 8).
Labellers saw the ground-truth final answer but no reference solution (p. 19).
Reward models are evaluated by best-of-N selection graded on the final answer, not by step-level agreement with held-out labels (p. 3).
Labellers were admitted after agreeing with the researchers' gold labels on at least 75% of 30 quality-control questions (p. 17).
Active learning that surfaces convincing wrong-answer solutions is about 2.6 times more data-efficient than uniform labelling (p. 2, p. 9).
The PRM also outperforms the ORM and majority voting on recent AP and AMC questions released after pre-training (72.9% against 63.8% and 61.3% at best-of-100; Table 1, p. 10).
The authors state that it is unknown how broadly the results generalise beyond math (p. 11).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: judging each step of a model's solution rather than only its final answer, and the observation that final-answer grading credits correct answers reached by incorrect reasoning (p. 5, p. 8), which EngTrace measures directly (93 of 228 correct-answer traces in X1 contain an incorrect step; state brief section 3). Lacks: generated instances (static MATH problems); gold traces (labels sit on model solutions, and labellers saw no reference solution, p. 19); deterministic step checks (all step labels are human, p. 3); the engineering domain (math only; generalisation beyond math 'unknown', p. 11); and validation of the step scorer against held-out expert labels (the PRM is validated only through best-of-N final-answer accuracy, p. 3, and labellers are screened rather than measured for agreement, p. 17). It is a training-signal paper, not a benchmark.
notes: Batch V question: Lightman et al. is the anchor citation for the planned paragraph on process supervision. What it says that bears on it: (a) the definitions of outcome and process supervision (pp. 1-2); (b) step correctness could not be automated, so 800K step labels were collected from human labellers (pp. 3-4), whereas EngTrace's templates compute the intermediate values, which is what lets E3's milestone match and E4's digit rule check part of each step deterministically, leaving only the residue to a judge (state brief section 2); (c) final-answer grading credits correct answers reached by incorrect reasoning (p. 5, p. 8), the failure EngTrace's X1 hard case quantifies; (d) supervision stops at the first wrong step (p. 6), whereas EngTrace's experts label every step; (e) the PRM is judged only by best-of-N final-answer selection (p. 3) and the labellers by a 75% screening threshold (p. 17), whereas EngTrace validates its step checks against 15 experts with measured agreement (Fleiss kappa 0.781 on steps; state brief section 3); (f) the authors call generalisation beyond math unknown (p. 11). The paper is also the origin of the data behind one of EngTrace's measured baselines: VersaPRM is a LoRA on Llama-PRM800K (state brief section 3), so PRM800K should be cited where that baseline is described. The paper says nothing about LLM judges. Given the deterministic evaluator with a residual judge, the revised text may cite it for (a), (b), (c) and (f) and as the source of PRM800K; not for a 'tiered' or 'two-stage' protocol, which it does not describe. Other notes: the abstract's '78%' is best-of-1860 selection on a 500-problem subset, not single-sample accuracy (p. 7, p. 18), and should not be quoted as a solve rate. The paper is internally inconsistent on its OOD set: '224 STEM questions' in the text against 45 + 60 + 45 + 84 = 234 in Table 1 (p. 10). 4.5K MATH test problems were moved into the PRM800K training set, which is why evaluation uses the remaining 500 (p. 5). The text is v1; the catalogue's ICLR 2024 venue is not shown in it.
